source.title: Small Batch Size Training for Language Models: When Vanilla SGD Works, and Why Gradient Accumulation Is Wasteful
source.authors: Martina Marek; Sanae Lotfi; A. Somasundaram; Andrew Gordon Wilson; Micah Goldblum

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests batch-size and optimizer effects on language-model validation loss, and argues that earlier reports of small-batch underperformance can result from incomplete hyperparameter tuning. It does not test the random-label memorization claim or the image-classifier versions.
record.gate_note: Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows. Figure 7 reports memory requirements, not a generalization outcome, so it is omitted. Figures 3–5 report robustness and scaling results; these do not directly measure the train–test gap, but bear on V5 through validation performance across batch sizes and training tokens.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own optimizer and batch-size comparisons on held-out language-model performance under fixed token budgets and five-epoch fine-tuning. These test V4 and V5 in modern transformer settings. Its strongest rebuttals concern small-batch instability and SGD inferiority, which are not themselves the supplied claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that appropriately tuned small batches can match or outperform larger batches, recommend the smallest batch maximizing throughput, and discourage gradient accumulation except when communication between model replicas is a bottleneck. They also advocate small-state optimizers for memory-constrained fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: Language-model pretraining and fine-tuning experiments comparing batch sizes and optimizer choices; the paper tunes or rescales optimizer hyperparameters and reports validation loss or task score, rather than testing the original claim's natural-label versus random-label generalization gap.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size, optimizer choice, optimizer hyperparameter tuning, and β2 scaling by second-moment token half-life affect reported validation performance. GPT-3 and GPT-2 results differ for batch-size-1 SGD.
record.problems: Most optimizer and batch-size comparisons use validation loss, not a directly reported train–test error gap. Several results are qualitative descriptions of figures without numerical values in the text. GPT-3 learning rates were not extensively tuned; the paper says tuning was computationally prohibitive.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3's Adam hyperparameter sensitivity ablation and Figure 4's learning-rate and decay-scaling sweeps were not entered as separate rows: these measure robustness and hyperparameter scaling rather than the batch-size generalization outcome named in V4 or V5. Figure 8's MATH-score bars are retained as a figure-only row, but cannot establish the direction or size of a performance difference from the text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out performance in the same architectures.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.

Image benchmarks; matched limited-tuning comparisons across the full optimizer set; equal-training-performance comparisons; switching from Adam to SGD; isolated decoupled-weight-decay recovery; word-level language models.

Image classifiers; extending training to recover large-batch performance; isolated normalization interventions. Fixed token budgets are tested and must not be listed as untested fixed-budget comparisons.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on dataset size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap correlations and comparisons with other predictors.

missing.what: GPT-3-style 1.3B results for batch-1 Adam and Adafactor: both outperform the default batch-512 AdamW baseline; scaling Adam's second-moment half-life improves its small-batch performance. Record separately from SGD parity.

GPT-2 AdamW comparison reports similar minimum validation loss at batches 1 and 512 after learning-rate and first-moment tuning, with weight decay removed and second-moment decay rescaled at batch 1. This is an additional adapted-recipe parity result.

Weight-precision ablation shows that stochastic rounding brings bfloat16 performance close to float32 even at the smallest batches, while deterministic rounding can penalize small batches. Record this precision-dependent batch-size condition.

record.verdict_notes: Held-out validation loss directly bears on V4 and V5; a separately reported train–test gap is unnecessary for these versions. Fixed-token pretraining comparisons use a single epoch, as Appendix B states. Equality after recipe adaptation qualifies the large-batch penalty rather than establishing a general contradiction. Figure 8 cannot support a directional verdict from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Image-classification benchmarks; broad tuning across all methods; decoupled weight decay and switching from Adam to SGD as recovery mechanisms; word-level language models.
Image-classification benchmarks; fixed-epoch comparisons across workload-dependent batch sizes; gradient-accumulation comparisons of held-out performance; normalization or regularization changes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other measured properties as predictors of the train–test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: 30M model
rows.operation_detail: Grid search over optimizer hyperparameters and batch sizes; compare lowest validation loss.

conditions.value: SGD, Adam, Adafactor, and Muon; hyperparameters jointly tuned per batch size

rows.value: All optimizers perform best at the smallest batch size; as batch size increases, each optimizer's performance degrades and the gap between optimizers widens.
rows.note: The paper describes the trend but does not give numerical loss values in the text.
rows.check: Split by optimizer and batch-size condition. For V5, increasing validation loss with batch size is observed under the same 600M-token budget. For V4, the optimizers perform similarly at small batches, while sophisticated optimizers gain an advantage at large batches; a single observed state cannot represent both comparisons. Tuning includes moment decay parameters, exceeding V4's limited-tuning condition.

source_check.correct: V5: observed; every optimizer's validation performance worsens as batch size increases at fixed 600M tokens. V4: optimizer performance is similar at small batches, while sophisticated optimizers gain an advantage at larger batches; separate these conditions rather than assigning partial to both versions.
source_check.problem: The shared partial state does not represent the full batch-size trend or the conditional optimizer comparison.

rows.subject: GPT-3 (1.3B)
rows.operation_detail: Train with batch size 1 using vanilla SGD without momentum; compare validation loss with the AdamW baseline.

rows.value: SGD performs on par with the AdamW baseline.
rows.note: Hyperparameter tuning of the learning rate for each optimizer was computationally prohibitive; SGD had a four-value learning-rate sweep.
rows.check: Reported parity shows neither an adaptive-optimizer disadvantage nor a large-batch penalty in this joint recipe comparison. Optimizer, batch size, weight decay and tuning differ, so neither factor's independent effect is identified. The subject is a modified GPT-3-style architecture.
